nodes.label: Bird's-eye view: command-line arguments and streams

edges.label: The topic 'Bird's-eye view: command-line arguments and streams' introduces stream_model.

[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday 'reading' (a page, a list) leaves the text in place so you can glance back at it; a Java input stream is consumed: each read removes the next value, and there is no going back.
[1] misconception (M) -> StdInRereads: wrong rule: Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice. Right rule: Each read consumes the value it returns, so a second StdIn.readInt() returns the next value in the stream (input 3 5 gives 3, then 5).
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> StdInRereads: Points to LT (reads take values from the front in order; prints append at the end in order). An uneven trace reuses an already-consumed value on some reads, or writes some output out of execution order. (here mixing in: "Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice")

[0] names_the_element (N): A stream is an I/O abstraction: an ordered sequence of values or characters, with no length limit from the program's point of view. Input is read from the front and output is appended at the end.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A Java program turns a standard input stream and command-line arguments into a standard output stream (plus drawing and audio). It consumes values when it reads them, so it cannot back up.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Input values are delivered strictly in stream order: each read removes the next value from the front. Output appears in the order the output calls execute, because each call appends to the end.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A read returns the next unread value, converted to the requested type. With input `3 5 7`, three StdIn.readInt() calls return 3, 5, 7. The output stream is the concatenation of all printed text in execution order.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One read advances the input position past exactly one value and returns it. One print appends its text to the output and returns nothing (void). No other state changes.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): All StdIn calls in a program share one input position. A read before a loop and reads inside the loop therefore take successive values, never the same one.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): All StdOut/System.out calls write to one output stream in execution order, and text already written cannot be taken back.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Streams let a program process an amount of data that is unbounded and not known in advance. They also decouple the program from the device. Plan: input-process-output (the 'filter' plan).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> StdInRereads: Changing where a stream comes from or goes to (keyboard, file, pipe, another device) keeps the program's behaviour. Changing the order of two reads swaps which value lands in which variable.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use the stream model when data are processed in one sequential pass, possibly of unknown or huge length. If the program must revisit values (sorting, k-th smallest), first save them in an array.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A read must be preceded by available input (the stream is finite and cannot be re-read). Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: More read calls than values in the stream, e.g. reading 3 values from input `4 7`.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Values are consumed once; to use a value again it must be stored in a variable or array. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Code that calls a read a second time expecting the same value (e.g. readInt() in a test and again in the body), so it silently skips values.
wrong: Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice. | right: The program consumes values when it reads them, so each call returns the next value.
wrong: Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice. | right: The program consumes values when it reads them, so each call returns the next value.
StdIn reads a stream: values arrive in order and each value is consumed once.
StdOut writes a stream: each print appends its text to the end of the output.
